Bayesian-Multiplicative and Count Zero Replacement

Source: R/replace_zeros.r
replace_zeros_cmult.Rd

Replaces the zeros of a count table with small proportions that depend on each sample's depth, and scales each sample's non-zero proportions down by the same factor, keeping their ratios. The methods of zCompositions' cmultRepl() (Martín-Fernández et al. 2015): geometric Bayesian-multiplicative (gbm, the usual choice), square-root Bayesian-multiplicative (sq), Bayes-Laplace Bayesian-multiplicative (bl), and count zero multiplicative (czm).

Usage

replace_zeros_gbm(counts, margin = 1L, frac = 0.65, adjust = TRUE)

replace_zeros_sq(counts, margin = 1L, frac = 0.65, adjust = TRUE)

replace_zeros_bl(counts, margin = 1L, frac = 0.65, adjust = TRUE)

replace_zeros_czm(
  counts,
  margin = 1L,
  frac = 0.65,
  threshold = 0.5,
  adjust = TRUE
)

Arguments

counts

A numeric matrix of non-negative counts (samples \(\times\) features), or any of the objects listed under Input Types. Each sample's total is its number of reads, so give counts, not proportions (other values give a warning).

margin

The margin containing samples. 1 if samples are rows, 2 if samples are columns. Ignored when counts is a special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1

frac

For czm, the fraction of the upper limit (threshold reads) that a zero becomes; and, with adjust, the fraction of a feature's smallest observed proportion that an imputed value above it becomes. Between 0 and 1 (exclusive). Default: 0.65.

adjust

If TRUE (the default), an imputed proportion above the smallest proportion observed for that feature in any sample is replaced by frac times that proportion, so that no zero is imputed above what was actually seen.

threshold

For czm, the upper limit of a zero, in reads: a zero in a sample of \(n\) reads is below threshold / n. Above 0 and at most 1. Default: 0.5.

Value

A dense numeric matrix of proportions with no zeros, in the orientation of counts (samples \(\times\) features for margin = 1, features \(\times\) samples for margin = 2, and for a single sample given as a vector), with its names. Each sample sums to 1. Attributes:

  • method: 'gbm', 'sq', 'bl' or 'czm'.

  • n_adjusted: the number of imputed values that adjust lowered.

  • n_replaced: the number of zeros replaced.

Details

For sample \(i\) with counts \(c_{ij}\), depth \(n_i = \sum_j c_{ij}\), proportions \(x_{ij} = c_{ij} / n_i\) and \(D\) features, each zero becomes a proportion \(r_{ij}\), and each non-zero proportion is scaled so that the sample sums to 1: $$r_{ij} = x_{ij} \Bigl(1 - \sum_{k:\, c_{ik} = 0} r_{ik}\Bigr) \quad \text{if } c_{ij} > 0.$$

Bayesian-multiplicative methods (gbm, sq, bl). A zero is the posterior estimate of a multinomial probability under a Dirichlet prior with expectation \(t_{ij}\) and strength \(s_i\): $$r_{ij} = \frac{s_i\, t_{ij}}{n_i + s_i} \quad \text{if } c_{ij} = 0.$$ The prior expectation is the feature's pooled proportion in the other samples, $$t_{ij} = \frac{\sum_{k \ne i} c_{kj}}{\sum_{k \ne i} n_k},$$ so a feature that is abundant elsewhere gets a larger value. The methods differ in the strength:

Method\(s_i\)
gbm\(1 / g_i\), with \(g_i\) the geometric mean of \(t_{i1}, \ldots, t_{iD}\)
sq\(\sqrt{n_i}\)
bl\(D\)

Count zero multiplicative (czm). Every zero of sample \(i\) becomes \(r_{ij} = frac \cdot threshold / n_i\): by default 65% of half a read. The other samples are used only by adjust.

Adjustment. With adjust = TRUE, an \(r_{ij}\) above \(m_j = \min_{k:\, c_{kj} > 0} x_{kj}\), the smallest proportion of feature \(j\) observed in any sample, becomes \(frac \cdot m_j\) (before the non-zero parts are scaled). This happens mostly in shallow samples.

Requirements. No sample may be all zeros. The Bayesian methods need at least two samples, and no feature may be zero in every sample (its prior would be 0). gbm also needs every feature to be non-zero in at least two samples: a feature seen in a single sample makes that sample's \(t_{ij}\) zero, its geometric mean zero and its prior strength infinite. Filter such features out first (e.g. counts[, colSums(counts > 0) >= 2]), or use sq or bl, which handle them. czm works on a single sample, and replaces the zeros of a feature that is zero everywhere like any other.

The proportion of zeros is not checked: features that are zeros in most samples, as are most features of a microbiome table, are imputed mostly from their prior. zCompositions warns about (or drops) rows and columns that are at least 80% zeros; ecodive never drops any.

Compared with zCompositions. The results equal cmultRepl(counts, method = ..., output = "prop", z.delete = FALSE) of zCompositions 1.6.2, to within about \(10^{-15}\) (relative). Unlike cmultRepl(), a table without zeros gives its proportions instead of an error, czm accepts a single sample and features that are zero everywhere, and czm refuses zeros whose imputed values would leave the sample's non-zero parts at zero or below.

The result feeds straight into aitchison(), alr(), ilr() and any function with norm = 'clr', with no pseudocount.

Input Types

The counts parameter is designed to accept a simple numeric matrix, but seamlessly supports objects from the following biological data packages:

  • phyloseq

  • rbiom

  • SummarizedExperiment

  • TreeSummarizedExperiment

For large datasets, standard matrix operations may be slow. See vignette('performance') for details on using optimized formats (e.g. sparse matrices) and parallel processing.

References

Martín-Fernández, J. A., Hron, K., Templ, M., Filzmoser, P., & Palarea-Albaladejo, J. (2015). Bayesian-multiplicative treatment of count zeros in compositional data sets. Statistical Modelling, 15, 134–158. doi:10.1177/1471082X14535524

Palarea-Albaladejo, J., & Martín-Fernández, J. A. (2015). zCompositions — R package for multivariate imputation of left-censored data under a compositional approach. Chemometrics and Intelligent Laboratory Systems, 143, 85–96. doi:10.1016/j.chemolab.2015.02.019

See also

replace_zeros(), replace_zeros_mult(), list_zero_replacements()

Examples

    # Geometric Bayesian-multiplicative replacement.
    x <- replace_zeros_gbm(ex_counts)
    x
#>        Streptococcus Bacteroides Corynebacterium Haemophilus Propionibacterium
#> Saliva   0.468724440 0.005786721     0.001056911 0.520804933      0.0028933607
#> Gums     0.894087889 0.004509901     0.001056911 0.098090349      0.0011274753
#> Nose     0.021760633 0.001978239     0.492581602 0.001978239      0.2482690406
#> Stool    0.001624823 0.992767072     0.001624823 0.001624823      0.0007336343
#>        Staphylococcus
#> Saliva   0.0007336343
#> Gums     0.0011274753
#> Nose     0.2334322453
#> Stool    0.0016248234
#> attr(,"method")
#> [1] "gbm"
#> attr(,"n_adjusted")
#> [1] 4
#> attr(,"n_replaced")
#> [1] 4

    # The ratios between non-zero parts are kept.
    nz <- ex_counts[1, ] > 0
    all.equal(x[1, nz] / sum(x[1, nz]), ex_counts[1, nz] / sum(ex_counts[1, nz]))
#> [1] TRUE

    # The other methods.
